title: Repeated recovery of structural load capacity after cracking

concept.text: The innovation is concrete that repeatedly regains structural load capacity after cracking severe enough to impair its performance. A beam or slab would recover useful strength and stiffness through a healing mechanism within the material, without requiring injection or patching after each damage event. The intended capability must work with practical reinforcement, under ordinary outdoor exposure, and at a cost comparable to ordinary concrete. This is a research target; the supplied evidence does not establish that the complete capability has been achieved.

The defining distinction is between closing a route for water or salts and restoring the ability to carry load. Crack sealing and reduced permeability can improve durability while leaving tensile or flexural recovery unproven. Conversely, retaining compressive strength does not establish recovery of strength lost through cracking. A proposed boundary example is a crack wider than about 0.3 mm that becomes watertight but remains mechanically weakened: that would satisfy a durability objective while leaving this structural objective unmet. The width is illustrative, not an established dividing line between durability and structural damage.

significance.text: Conditional significance: repeated recovery of design strength and stiffness could change how some damaged structures are maintained. Instead of every consequential crack necessarily triggering a material repair, engineers could sometimes verify that an internal healing process had restored the required performance. Bridges, tunnels, retaining structures, and marine infrastructure are motivating applications because cracking can create pathways for water and salts and contribute to reinforcement deterioration. These are engineering motivations in the supplied research, rather than outcomes verified by the retained source evidence.

The direct benefit would be recovery of mechanical performance after damage, extending the purpose of healing beyond slowing the ingress of harmful substances. Reduced repair interventions, longer useful service, and lower lifecycle emissions are conditional downstream possibilities. Their magnitude would depend on healing reliability, exposure, reinforcement condition, concrete cover, maintenance practice, and the cost and carbon intensity of the healing system. The supplied material establishes no numerical benefit, including a 200-year service life or lifecycle CO2 reductions greater than half.

Capacity recovery would not automatically make structural reliability independent of detecting cracks. Engineers would still need to establish how quickly recovery occurs, what loads are safe during healing, whether damage remains, and whether reinforcement, bond, or fatigue performance has deteriorated. An intrinsic, autonomous healing mechanism is a useful conceptual description of the target, but the supplied record does not verify its historical attribution. The analogy also has limits: restoring a crack interface does not necessarily regenerate every damaged component of a reinforced member.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unsolved capability to be established is repeatable restoration of meaningful member-level capacity under realistic exposure and loading, at ordinary-concrete cost. The supplied evidence does not establish either a successful demonstration or the present-day absence of one. The central scientific challenge is to connect healing at a crack to renewed load transfer across that crack, then demonstrate that the resulting member has recovered the required tensile or flexural performance rather than merely becoming less permeable.

Engineering synthesis: a successful system would need to retain a useful healing capability after the first event, including when damage reopens an earlier crack or forms elsewhere. Concrete barriers to investigate include depletion or loss of access to healing agents, weak or incomplete bonding across crack faces, dependence on favorable moisture and temperature, and insufficient recovery time between damaging loads. Tests must also resolve whether apparent recovery reflects continued curing or other background changes rather than the intended healing mechanism.

Structural integration adds further barriers. Recovery of the concrete alone may leave reinforcement damage, loss of bond, residual deformation, or fatigue degradation unresolved. Scaling a successful specimen to a reinforced beam or slab also requires compatibility with mixing, placement, curing, and practical member dimensions. The research attributes gaps in standardized testing, long-term stability, compatibility, and scale-up cost to the September 2025 review, but its source text was not captured, so these remain reported findings rather than independently verified conclusions here.

current_state.text: The supplied bibliography identifies a review by Hassan Tumwiine, Teshome Chala, Henry Ssenyonjo, Derrick Kirigoola, and Amin Al-Fakih, titled “On the use of self-healing materials in concrete technology: A comprehensive review of materials, mechanisms, and field applications,” listed as Materials Today Chemistry 48, article 103001, September 2025. The research describes abstract-level publisher access. However, the source index records no captured document or retained artifact, and the validated review had no abstract or full text available for checking. The findings below therefore describe what the research reports from that review; they are not independently confirmed source passages.

The research reports that existing systems seal microcracks and, in some cases, cracks approaching roughly 1 mm, with improvements in transport properties. It attributes to the review a distinction between generally retained compressive strength and more limited tensile and flexural recovery, together with greater effectiveness of autonomous systems for wider cracks above approximately 0.3–0.5 mm. These quantitative width claims cannot be checked against the uncaptured source. Even if confirmed, a reported sealing width would not by itself establish the magnitude of restored load capacity, recovery time, repeatability, or performance under service exposure.

The research also attributes field applications in tunnels, retaining walls, and marine works to the review. Those reports may indicate practical deployment of healing materials, but the supplied record gives no project-level test results, damage histories, recovery cycles, or structural measurements. It therefore cannot establish that these applications demonstrated repeated recovery of lost structural capacity. Equally, the absence of retained source content is not evidence that the reported applications or material capabilities are false.

The supplied record contains no independently assessable demonstration of the complete target and no search history establishing the state of the field after the listed September 2025 review. It supports neither a claim that repeated structural recovery in service has been achieved nor a definitive claim that it remains undemonstrated everywhere. No supplied result is identified as a preprint or a disputed experimental finding; the central limitation is unavailable source content and unassessed freshness.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: use full-scale beams or slabs with reinforcement representative of practice. Introduce controlled cracking that produces a pre-agreed, design-relevant loss of flexural capacity and document the resulting stiffness, deformation, and crack pattern. Allow the material to heal under outdoor wet-dry exposure without injection or patching, then demonstrate recovery mechanically. Repeat consequential damage and recovery more than once. Small coupons healed in limewater could support mechanism development, but would not establish this full structural and environmental scope.
completion_criteria.label: Full-scale reinforced members repeatedly recover flexural capacity under outdoor exposure

completion_criteria.text: Proposed protocol: specify the initial damage fraction, required recovery fraction, healing time, cycle count, loading history, and acceptable residual damage before testing begins. Measure strength and stiffness separately, and record reinforcement and bond condition. Because measuring ultimate capacity can itself destroy or substantially alter a specimen, the protocol should use appropriately matched specimens or another justified measurement strategy to avoid confusing verification damage with the next planned cycle. Include controls that distinguish healing from continued curing and other background changes.
completion_criteria.label: Predeclared protocols separately verify strength and stiffness recovery against controls

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: repeat the demonstration across independent specimens and laboratories, with documented mixtures, reinforcement details, exposure histories, and measurement methods. Establish the loads that can safely be carried during recovery and the consequences of incomplete or failed healing. Report which crack widths, damage severities, exposure conditions, and loading regimes were tested. Finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth within those conditions, rather than universal healing across all damage and environments.
completion_criteria.label: Independent laboratories reproduce recovery and establish safe operating boundaries

completion_criteria.text: Proposed economic criterion: compare the binder and healing-system cost with an explicitly defined ordinary-concrete baseline, and separately report installation, quality-control, monitoring, and maintenance implications. Cost reporting alone would not demonstrate cost parity; an agreed acceptable premium or parity requirement must be tested. All damage, recovery, cycle, and cost thresholds described here are proposed acceptance criteria, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Binder and healing-system costs meet agreed ordinary-concrete cost limits

related_concepts.text: CIV-05, “Tensile-ductile mineral structures that replace reinforced concrete at ordinary cost,” concerns ductility and replacement of conventional reinforced construction. CIV-04 concerns recovery after capacity has been lost. A material that distributes deformation across fine cracks could help control damage and make healing more feasible, but ductility or fine cracking alone would not demonstrate repeated recovery. The earlier research described CIV-05 specifically through strain-hardening composites; the supplied roster supports the broader ductility distinction without establishing that particular implementation.

CIV-11, “Default-cost reinforcement with carbon-steel behavior and no corrosion in ordinary exposures,” addresses reinforcement durability. Preventing corrosion could complement CIV-04 by removing one source of deterioration after cracking, but it would not by itself close cracks or restore the concrete’s lost mechanical performance. Conversely, healing concrete would not automatically repair already damaged reinforcement. The concepts remain separate even where their benefits reinforce each other.

CIV-07, “Load-bearing engineered living materials for ordinary structures,” overlaps where a biological mechanism contributes to healing. Its defining objective is an engineered living material that bears structural loads; CIV-04 is defined by repeated mechanical recovery and can, in principle, use biological or nonbiological mechanisms. CIV-01, “A primary structural binder at global cement scale without process carbon dioxide,” addresses binder production and process emissions. A low-emission binder might host a healing system, but neither emissions performance nor healing establishes the other capability.

CIV-09, “Immediate building occupancy after the design earthquake, at life-safety cost,” and CIV-12, “Fail-safe adaptive primary structural response at ordinary-building cost,” share interests in structural performance after or during damaging events. CIV-04 could contribute to later recovery, but a healing delay would not establish immediate occupancy, and material healing would not itself establish adaptive structural response. These are complementary system-level objectives with different timing and performance requirements.

unresolved_issues: The review’s bibliographic identity and reported findings have not been verified from captured source content. The research reports abstract-level access, while the source index contains no retained artifact.
The precise conditions, healing times, mechanical recovery measurements, and repeatability behind the reported crack-width capabilities remain unknown.
The reported field applications lack project-level evidence showing whether they measured sealing, transport properties, structural recovery, or repeated recovery.
The supplied record does not establish whether later work has demonstrated the complete target; freshness remains unassessed.
Damage fraction, recovery fraction, cycle count, safe loads during healing, exposure envelope, and acceptable cost premium remain to be defined for a convincing demonstration.

The validated review’s blanket conclusion that CIV-05 and CIV-11 were undefined was not adopted because their titles are supplied in the roster. Comparisons remain limited to those titles; the specific strain-hardening implementation previously associated with CIV-05 is not established.
The historical attribution of the intrinsic, autonomous healing description remains unverified.

brief.title: Concrete that regains strength after repeated cracking
possible: A cracked bridge beam or tunnel slab could regain useful strength and resistance to bending through a healing process inside the concrete. It could recover after repeated damage, without crews injecting or patching each crack.
The concrete would work with the steel reinforcement used in construction, endure ordinary outdoor conditions and cost about as much as ordinary concrete.
why: Engineers could sometimes confirm that a damaged structure had recovered the performance it needed, reducing the need for material repairs. Bridges, tunnels and marine structures could stay useful longer, with fewer repair interventions and lower emissions over their lives.

sources.showed: This review covers materials, healing mechanisms and field applications of concrete that repairs its own cracks.
sources.cited_for: It surveys approaches to crack healing and barriers to practical use.
sources.not_established: Crack sealing alone does not establish repeated recovery of lost strength.

sources.showed: They built a network of tubes carrying repair material inside concrete and demonstrated repeated healing in bending tests. Some specimens regained stiffness, or resistance to bending, but recovered little strength.
sources.quote: self-healing and multiple self-healing is possible with this developed vascular system.
sources.cited_for: Internal delivery of repair material can support repeated mechanical recovery in laboratory tests.
sources.not_established: The tests do not establish repeated outdoor recovery in full-size reinforced members; the network also allows external refilling.

sources.who: Zhigang Zhang, Qian Zhang and Victor C. Li
sources.showed: They found recovery of strength and stiffness in a cement mixture reinforced with small fibers. Healing restored friction between fibers and the surrounding material, helping fibers carry force across cracks.
sources.quote:
At the meso-scale, self-healing leads to ﬁber bridging strength recovery to
about the same level as that of virgin specimens.
sources.cited_for: Healing can restore mechanical performance through renewed force transfer across cracks.
sources.not_established: The work does not establish repeated recovery in full-size reinforced structures under ordinary outdoor exposure.

sources.showed: In thin beams made from high-performance concrete, cracks opened more slowly under repeated loading after underwater healing.
sources.quote: showed up to twenty times reduction in the rate of crack opening displacement as compared to the same specimen before the healing period.
sources.cited_for: Healing can improve resistance to crack growth under repeated loading.
sources.not_established: Underwater healing of thin beams does not establish repeated recovery of full structural capacity outdoors.

shown: Minnebo and colleagues demonstrated repeated mechanical repair in laboratory bending tests using internal tubes that deliver repair material. Their results also show why strength and stiffness need separate measurements: stiffness can recover while strength remains limited.

Zhang and colleagues linked mechanical recovery in fiber-reinforced cement to renewed friction around the fibers. Kannikachalam and colleagues found slower crack opening under repeated loads after underwater healing. These are parts of the capability, demonstrated under different test conditions.
missing: Full-size reinforced beams or slabs would need to regain useful strength and stiffness repeatedly outdoors without patching or injection.
Controlled tests would need to separate healing from continued curing and measure remaining damage to reinforcement and its grip on concrete.
Independent laboratories would need to reproduce recovery and establish safe loads while healing occurs.
The binder and healing system would need to meet an agreed cost limit comparable to ordinary concrete.

milestones.label: Full-size reinforced members repeatedly recover outdoors
milestones.explanation: Full-size reinforced beams or slabs would have to recover bending strength repeatedly after consequential cracking under outdoor wet-dry exposure. This would connect laboratory healing to structural use.

milestones.label: Controlled tests establish strength and stiffness recovery separately
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to set recovery criteria beforehand, measure strength and stiffness separately, and compare with specimens without healing. This would distinguish repair from continued curing or damage caused by testing.

milestones.label: Independent laboratories reproduce recovery and define safe limits
milestones.explanation: Independent laboratories would have to reproduce recovery and establish safe loads during healing across stated damage and exposure conditions. This would define where engineers could rely on the material.

milestones.label: Material costs meet agreed ordinary-concrete limits
milestones.explanation: Binder and healing-system costs would have to meet an agreed limit against ordinary concrete, with installation and monitoring costs reported separately. This would establish whether the material meets its affordability target.

uncertain: It remains unclear how long healing stays effective when cracks reopen or new cracks form elsewhere.
Required recovery, healing time, acceptable remaining damage and safe loads during healing still need agreed thresholds.
The moisture and temperature conditions needed for reliable recovery remain open questions.

page.title: Repeated mechanical self-healing of concrete
page.definition: Concrete in a steel-reinforced member regains specified flexural capacity and stiffness after repeated cracking, using healing resources installed before damage. Flexural capacity is resistance to bending; stiffness is resistance to deformation.

goal.need: RM4L’s September 2022 report cites UK expenditure of £40 billion a year on maintaining mostly concrete infrastructure, drawing on 2016 Office for National Statistics data. Repeated mechanical healing targets recovery of the load-carrying function after damage. RILEM distinguishes this function from closing cracks. The expenditure describes the maintenance context; it does not quantify savings achievable through self-healing.

statements.body: Resilient Materials for Life (RM4L), an EPSRC-funded research programme
statements.quote: Self-healing of time-dependent and cyclic loading damage
statements.context: Research Theme 2 in the programme’s September 2022 report.

statements.body: HEALCON, a European Union FP7 research project
statements.quote: Demonstration of the developed technologies in a real size structure
statements.context: Objective 6 in the final project report, last updated on 21 June 2017.

completion.title: A reinforced concrete member meets its mechanical requirements after two outdoor healing cycles.
completion.criterion: A full-size steel-reinforced concrete beam or slab again meets its specified flexural resistance and stiffness requirements after each of at least two separate cracking–healing events under its declared outdoor exposure. Each cracking event must first reduce those properties below the requirements. Healing uses only resources installed before damage, without crack injection or patching. Mechanical load tests distinguish healing from residual capacity and continued curing. The two-event minimum operationalizes repeated recovery; it is not an externally agreed acceptance threshold.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; the searched external documents do not establish an acceptance test for repeated mechanical recovery of reinforced concrete members.
completion.basis: Searches of RILEM guidance, ASTM listings, EN 1504 repair standards, and HEALCON and RM4L documents found no acceptance test specifying repeated member-level recovery. This fallback combines RILEM’s mechanical-healing distinction with the programmes’ cyclic-damage and real-size demonstration goals. Required resistance and stiffness remain specific to the member; no common recovery percentage, healing duration or exposure envelope was found.

milestones.title: Cracked concrete regains tensile or flexural strength in a mechanical reloading test.
milestones.criterion: Reloading establishes recovery of tensile or flexural strength attributable to healing, rather than crack closure alone. HEALCON evaluates recovery against same-age uncracked and cracked-unhealed specimens. Minnebo and colleagues reported first-reload flexural strength equal to 34% of initial strength for concrete containing inorganic phosphate cement capsules, compared with 15% for reference beams, with two specimens per group. These percentages include residual strength.
milestones.set_by: Mechanical-healing convention described in RILEM’s “RELEVANCE of STAR 221-SHC”, operationalized through HEALCON’s mechanical-recovery comparisons; no minimum recovery percentage is specified.
milestones.threshold_quote: Self-healing is not only about self-closing of cracks but the actual regaining of tensile or flexural strength.

milestones.title: Cracked concrete shows mechanical recovery after two laboratory healing intervals.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate mechanical recovery at both reloadings after two 24 h healing intervals; the published three-point bending protocol uses a crack opening of 300 µm. Inorganic phosphate cement vascular networks in concrete beams, with two specimens, produced first/second reload strength ratios of 92.3%/99% and stiffness ratios of 126%/96%, relative to initial loading. These ratios include residual capacity. The networks were emptied using pressure and refilled between loadings.
milestones.set_by: Minnebo and colleagues, Materials (2017), sections 3.1 and 3.3: a published capsule and vascular-network experimental protocol, not a consensus acceptance level.
milestones.threshold_quote: Two loading cycles, with a 24 h healing period in between, follow the initial bending

milestones.title: A full-size reinforced member recovers its specified capacity and stiffness once outdoors.
milestones.criterion: A full-size reinforced concrete member regains its specified flexural resistance and stiffness after one outdoor cracking–healing event that reduced both below specification, using healing resources installed before damage. HEALCON requires larger-scale and field verification but supplies no mechanical pass level. The paper published on 4 September 2018 describing the A465 trial reports five reinforced panels, four with six-month reloading results; the comparison provided no evidence of strength regain attributable to self-healing.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback for mechanical recovery in a full-size outdoor member; HEALCON’s demonstration objective does not define a mechanical acceptance threshold.

not_found: No external acceptance test was found specifying the recovery fraction, healing duration, cycle count and outdoor exposure required for repeated recovery of reinforced-member capacity.
No external ordinary-concrete cost-parity requirement was found for this capability.

No opened source establishes achievement of the completion test.

results.finding: Two IPC capsule concrete beams reached 34% of initial flexural strength on first reload.
results.detail: Reference beams reached 15%. The ratios include residual strength; the comparison supports recovery attributable to healing.

results.finding: Two IPC vascular concrete beams reached 99% of initial strength on second reload.
results.detail: First-reload strength was 92.3%; stiffness ratios were 126% and 96%. The three-point bending protocol used a 300 µm crack opening and two 24 h healing intervals. Ratios include residual capacity; the networks were emptied and refilled between loadings.

results.finding: Three self-healed ECC specimens recovered 98% of undamaged specimens’ single-crack fiber bridging strength.
results.detail: After 10 wet–dry cycles, the specimens were reloaded in tension. A same-age pre-cracked group without wet–dry exposure provided an unhealed comparison.
results.quote:
At the meso scale, the maximum ﬁber bridging stress in self-healed
ECC was found to restore to almost the same level (98%) as that of
the undamaged samples, whereas a substantial reduction in bridging
capacity is observed in un-healed pre-damaged samples.

results.finding: Underwater-healed UHPC beams, sample size not stated, showed up to a 20-fold reduction in crack-opening growth rate.
results.detail: The beams were reloaded in flexural fatigue after healing. The reported reduction in crack-opening growth rate does not establish recovery of tensile or flexural strength.
results.quote: The three-month healed specimens showed up to twenty times reduction in the rate of crack opening displacement as compared to the same specimen before the healing period.
